newsitem.title: USA: Democrats threaten all-night session on aid bill.
newsitem.headline: Democrats threaten all-night session on aid bill.

text.p: Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle threatened to hold the Senate in an all-night session Wednesday unless Republican leaders permit quick passage of disaster relief for the flood-ravaged upper Midwest.

"Nothing ought to have a higher priority," the North Dakota Democrat said at a news conference with the mayors of Grand Forks, North Dakota, and East Grand Forks, Minnesota. Both cities were among the hardest hit by floods that left thousands homeless and devastated businesses.

"If we have to stay in all night tonight, we are prepared to do that," Daschle said. He reiterated his threat to hold up passage of other legislation with lengthy debate until the disaster measure is cleared.
The measure is stalled in both the House and Senate over the issue of whether it should go to the White House with extraneous provisions certain to attract a presidential veto.

The collision course holds political risks for both sides. Republicans said a veto would delay the flow of disaster relief funds even more while Democrats put the blame on Republicans since they have refused to allow votes on a non-controversial funding bill.

House Republicans meeting on the issue Wednesday morning refused to drop the most controversial item, which they said was aimed at averting a government shutdown this fall. President Clinton has said he would veto the bill, sending it back to Congress for reconsideration, if it arrives with this unrelated anti-shutdown provision.
House Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner of Ohio told reporters after the meeting they will not remove the anti-shutdown provision.

"We still continue to believe that it should include a continuing resolution to prevent any possibility of a government shutdown come Sept. 30," he said. "We also believe that bill will be on the floor of the House and Senate before the week is over and we'll send it to the president."

The bill would allocate about $5 billion to about 30 states hit by natural disasters such as floods, mudslides and harsh weather. It also provides another $1.9 billion for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and continued U.S. military flights in the Persian Gulf.
Asked what would happen if it is vetoed, Boehner said: "We'll wait and see what the president decides to do."

If the disaster relief legislation is vetoed, it could be revised and sent back to Clinton the same day, Daschle noted. "Our desire is to get this process moving. Let's at least get the veto over with," he added.

A Republican aide said this week it was hoped the issue could be resolved quickly after Clinton vetoed the bill and that the House would then pass a disaster-relief measure with the government shutdown provision stripped out.
